results.result: Participants were trained on nine sequences consisting of unique combinations of three spatial and three temporal features over 3 days. Training resulted in significant RT improvements for trained sequences (410 ms to 288 ms) compared to smaller improvements for untrained sequences (456 ms to 346 ms), with error rates also decreasing more for trained sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C38 provide comprehensive behavioral data showing sequence-specific learning. The experimental design (C28-C29), RT measurements (C31-C34), error rates (C35-C36), and consistency across sessions (C37-C38) are well-documented with appropriate statistics and demonstrate successful training.

results.result: Post-test results revealed behavioral transfer of both spatial and temporal features to new sequence combinations. Sequences with trained spatial features showed immediate RT advantages, while trained temporal features showed delayed RT advantages. Both trained spatial (F(1,28)=20.830, p=0.0001) and temporal (F(1,28)=12.963, p=0.001) features were performed faster than untrained sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 demonstrate independent representation of spatial and temporal features through behavioral transfer. The statistical evidence (C43-C44) and pattern of immediate vs. delayed transfer (C39-C40) support the conclusion of independent storage (C42, C45). The lack of group differences (C46) strengthens the findings.

results.result: The delayed temporal transfer effect is explained by a multiplicative model where temporal representation acts as a go signal on a concrete spatial plan, requiring spatial expectation to manifest.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 provide a theoretical interpretation of the delayed temporal transfer supported by prior work (Kornysheva et al., 2013). The model is consistent with the behavioral data showing immediate spatial but delayed temporal transfer, though it remains a theoretical interpretation rather than direct experimental evidence.

results.result: Visually cued production of trained finger sequences yielded increased fMRI activation in motor areas (contralateral M1, PMd, bilateral SMA, PMv), ipsilateral cerebellum (lobule V-VI), and visual areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 describe standard activation results from fMRI analysis. These are straightforward observations of brain regions showing increased activity during the task compared to rest, providing context for the subsequent classification analyses.

results.result: The overall classifier detected sequence-specific representations in contralateral M1, PMd, PMv, bilateral SMA, superior parietal cortices, ipsilateral cerebellum (lobules V-VI), and visual areas. Results were consistent with prior work using faster sequences produced from memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C65 describe the overall classifier results validated by simulations (C57). The widespread activation pattern (C58-C62) with contralateral dominance (C63) is well-documented and consistent with prior work (C64). This establishes that sequence representations exist before testing for their specific encoding properties.

results.result: Only the contralateral M1 (handknob area) showed significant integrated encoding of spatio-temporal sequences (p=0.0005, Bonferroni corrected), with no significant integrated encoding in premotor regions (p>0.155).
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 present the key finding of integrated encoding exclusively in contralateral M1. The statistical evidence from both whole-brain (C66) and ROI analyses (C67-C68) with appropriate corrections supports this conclusion. This is a central result distinguishing M1 from premotor areas.

results.result: Spatial and temporal classifiers showed significant above-chance accuracy in premotor areas (bilateral PMd, contralateral SMA, ipsilateral PMv) and parietal regions, indicating independent representation of spatial and temporal features in bilateral premotor cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 demonstrate independent encoding in premotor areas through spatial and temporal classifier results. The statistical evidence from whole-brain analysis (C69-C70) supports the inference of independent representation (C71), contrasting with the integrated encoding in M1.

results.result: A significant ROI × hemisphere × classifier interaction (F(1,30)=12.808, p=0.001) confirmed differential encoding between M1 and premotor areas, with similar patterns for left and right hand training groups (no group interaction, p=0.75).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 provide statistical confirmation of the differential encoding between M1 and premotor areas through ANOVA. The lack of group interaction (C73) and similar distribution across hands (C74) strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: Center of gravity analysis revealed spatial gradients in encoding: integrated encoding was more caudal (toward M1) while independent encoding was more rostral (toward premotor areas) in the precentral region, with the reverse pattern postcentral. These effects were significant (precentral: F(1,30)=6.417, p=0.017; postcentral: F(1,30)=13.394, p=0.001) and consistent across training groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C81 demonstrate anatomical gradients in encoding types using CoG analysis. The statistical evidence (C76, C79) and consistency across groups (C77, C80) support the conclusion of differential representation across motor and premotor areas (C81). This provides spatial precision to the encoding differences.

results.result: Within premotor cortex, temporal and spatial representations showed partial overlap but with a functional gradient: temporal encoding was more ventral (PMv) and spatial encoding more dorsal (PMd), with a significant main effect (F(1,30)=5.836, p=0.022) consistent across hemispheres and groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C88 describe a dorsal-ventral gradient within premotor cortex. The CoG analysis (C84-C86) provides statistical support for the gradient, though the effect is more subtle than the M1-premotor distinction. The overlap (C82) and gradient (C88) together characterize premotor organization.

results.result: Control analyses ruled out that classification reflected simple finger tuning or temporal response profiles. The differential distribution of encoding types across brain regions (C90), insensitivity of the main response function to temporal profiles (C91-C92), and significant three-way interactions for spatial (F(1,31)=9.165, p=0.005) and temporal (F(1,31)=5.395, p=0.027) encoding between response type, ROI, and hemisphere support that voxel patterns reflect sequence-specific encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C98 address important methodological concerns about what the classifiers detect. The logical arguments (C89-C90), experimental design features (C91-C93), derivative analysis results (C94-C97), and statistical evidence (C96-C97) collectively support that the patterns reflect sequence encoding rather than confounds.

results.result: Although systematic force differences between sequences existed and could classify sequences (mean zacc=2.25, t(31)=10.914, p<0.001), force differences did not correlate with classification accuracy in contralateral M1 (r=-0.210, p=0.257), ruling out force as an explanation for integrated encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 address a potential confound. The presence of force differences (C99-C100) but lack of correlation with M1 classification (C101) supports the inference that force cannot explain the findings (C102). This strengthens the interpretation of sequence-specific encoding.

results.result: Classification accuracy in contralateral M1 correlated with sequence-specific learning (r=0.468, p=0.008), with participants showing higher learning also showing higher classification accuracy. No such relationship existed for ipsilateral M1 (r<-0.222, p>0.186), indicating contralateral M1 encoding relates to skill level.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 link neural encoding to behavioral performance. The significant correlation in contralateral M1 (C103-C104) and absence in ipsilateral M1 (C105) support the inference that encoding relates to skill (C106). This provides functional validation of the classification results.

results.result: The integrated sequence encoding in contralateral M1 is consistent with prior electrophysiology showing 40% of M1 neurons tuned to sequence commands, inactivation studies disrupting sequential behavior, and dynamical systems models proposing that each spatio-temporal sequence is controlled by distinct neuronal subpopulations forming dynamical networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 contextualize the M1 findings within prior literature. The citations to electrophysiology (C107), inactivation studies (C108), and correlation with learning (C109-C110) support the interpretation. The connection to dynamical systems theory (C111-C113) provides a theoretical framework consistent with the data.

results.result: Integrated encoding in M1 alone cannot explain behavioral flexibility in transferring spatial or temporal features independently. Higher-order motor areas (premotor cortices) parsed sequences into constituent features, providing a modular feature-separating storage consistent with observed behavioral flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 connect the neural findings to behavioral observations. The logical argument that integrated encoding cannot explain transfer (C114, C116) combined with behavioral evidence (C115) and neural evidence of independent encoding in premotor areas (C117-C118) support this interpretation linking structure to function.

results.result: The findings may not generalize to all movement classes. Continuous movements (e.g., reaching with force perturbations) show integrated learning, while discrete sequential movements show compelling evidence for independent temporal representation. The orthogonal design is unlikely to have artificially induced the effect, as similar flexibility was observed in prior studies with different designs.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 appropriately discuss generalizability. The distinction between movement types (C120-C122) is supported by citations, and the argument against design artifacts (C123) is strengthened by reference to prior work. This provides appropriate caveats while defending the validity of the findings.

results.result: The representational analysis method, validated by simulations, can distinguish integrated from independent representations even when spatially overlapping. The approach assumes linear additivity of BOLD signals from independent neuronal populations, which is reasonable for the restricted range of activity variation observed, and the M1-PMd dissociation likely reflects neural rather than hemodynamic differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C132 address methodological foundations. The validation by simulation (C127-C128), justification of linearity assumption for the restricted range (C129-C131), and argument for neural vs. hemodynamic interpretation (C132) support the validity of the approach. However, the linearity assumption remains a limitation that could affect interpretation.

results.result: The findings predict that premotor neurons tuned to spatial movement order (as shown by Tanji & Shima) should be independent of exact timing, and that independent temporal encoding exists in the same areas. Specifically, changing temporal intervals should not interfere with spatial sequence tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C138 make predictions about single-neuron responses based on the fMRI findings.
